narrative:
The model estimates you have a 49% chance of leaving your job. This is high enough that the company has decided to deny your promotion, as they are concerned you may not stay long-term.

The prediction is driven primarily by three key factors about your background. First, your relatively short overall work experience of 1-5 years was the strongest reason the model leaned toward you leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay have longer track records, so your limited experience across all jobs pulled the prediction toward departure. Second, the fact that you have not received other job offers while working here also contributed to expecting you might leave, though this had a milder effect. Surprisingly, this absence of external opportunities made the model slightly more likely to predict turnover rather than retention.

Working against these factors was your difficult work-life balance. While most employees predicted to stay report a medium balance, your struggle to balance work and personal life actually pushed the model slightly toward thinking you would remain, perhaps because it signals deep investment despite the strain.

The organization should consider discussing your career goals openly with you and exploring ways to build your experience faster through targeted responsibilities. You, in turn, may want to reflect on what would make you feel more anchored here. Addressing these areas could improve both your satisfaction and your chances in future promotion reviews.
